title: A Two-Person Startup Has Fixed One of the Most Hated Sounds in Modern Life
gist: Starling, a two-person sound-design studio (Joel Corelitz and Colin Coogan), showed that the hated beeps of nearly every microwave can be fixed purely with firmware changes to the same cheap piezo buzzer already inside the appliance, no new hardware required, reopening a bigger conversation about appliance makers' underinvestment in audio UX.

insights.claim: Nearly all microwaves use the same cheap component, a passive piezoelectric buzzer costing a matter of cents, to generate their beeps, and manufacturers avoid swapping it for pricier speakers because white-goods competition runs on thin margins.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Explains why an entire product category has tolerated bad UX for decades purely on cost grounds, exposing a low-cost differentiation opportunity for any manufacturer willing to invest a little in software.
insights.quote: Competition in consumer white goods is fierce. Why replace a super-cheap part that does the job with something pricier?
insights.locator: But the reason the vast majority of microwave manufacturers stubbornly stick with offensive beeps

insights.claim: The piezoelectric buzzer was brought to mass market by Japanese manufacturers in the 1970s and, due to its low cost and simplicity, spread into toys, smoke detectors, alarm clocks, multimeters, watches, and microwaves, though manufacturers can only control its frequency and duration.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: The same commodity component and constraint set is embedded across many device categories beyond microwaves, meaning the same firmware-only sound fix could plausibly be applied to a much wider installed base of consumer electronics.
insights.locator: The piezo buzzer was first brought to the mass market in the 1970s

insights.claim: Starling proved that dramatically better, more distinctive microwave sounds can be produced entirely by rewriting the C++ firmware running on a microwave's existing microcontroller and piezo buzzer, with no added hardware or bill-of-materials cost.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A zero-hardware-cost margin lever: appliance makers could differentiate on sound purely through a firmware update, making this an easy, high-ROI product improvement to watch for adoption.
insights.quote: Any microcontroller that accepts C++ can take different programming and produce different sounds
insights.locator: Any microcontroller that accepts C++ can take different programming

insights.claim: Corelitz found that sweeping a piezo buzzer's output to its resonant frequency range makes it sound louder without any actual volume change, letting sound designers fake dynamic loudness on hardware that has no real volume control.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A specific, reusable audio-engineering trick that turns a hard hardware limitation (fixed loudness) into a software-solvable problem, useful IP for any consultancy licensing sound design to appliance OEMs.
insights.quote: If you sweep through the frequencies, you'll notice that at a certain frequency range the buzzers just sound louder, because they prefer that resonance
insights.locator: Corelitz has a way to fake volume from piezo tech

insights.claim: To eliminate beep fatigue from repeated menu button presses, Starling replaced it with a soft, roughly 4,000-Hz, one-millisecond click modeled on smartphone touch-typing sounds, showing that single-parameter tweaks (frequency, duration) can materially change perceived product quality.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Illustrates how minor, near-zero-cost parameter changes to existing components can be an easy, low-risk differentiation lever across many device categories, not just microwaves.
insights.quote: I just wanted to see what a 4,000-Hz beep for one millisecond would sound like
insights.locator: To banish repetitive harsh beeps when pressing multiple buttons

themes.theme: Willingness to pay for sound design

insights.claim: In response to Starling's sonic demos posted on Instagram, a recurring comment was that people would pay roughly $50 more for a microwave that sounded better, suggesting appliance sound design could become a monetizable premium feature rather than a pure cost center.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A concrete price-premium signal (~$50) that appliance manufacturers or investors could test as a real pricing lever for better audio UX in white goods.
insights.quote: One of the top things that people kept commenting over and over again was, ‘Oh my God, I would pay $50 more for a microwave that sounded better,’
insights.locator: One of the top things that people kept commenting

insights.claim: Richard Hughes, Volvo's design lead for digital user experiences and a 15-year principal UX designer at Whirlpool, says most appliance manufacturers invest engineering effort in reducing product noise but have little to no internal sound-design expertise.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific organizational skills gap inside large appliance OEMs (audio UX) that outside sound-design consultancies like Starling could fill or be acquired to fix.
insights.quote: A lot of these companies don't have internal audio expertise
insights.locator: A lot of these companies don't have internal audio expertise

insights.claim: While at Whirlpool, Hughes experimented with piezo-and-Arduino sound design similarly to Starling and helped launch a premium KitchenAid Pro Line toaster whose softer piezo tone became known among users as its 'flight attendant call button' sound, but this care was never extended to Whirlpool's microwaves.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A real internal case study showing better appliance sound design already had positive market reception at a major OEM when applied to a premium product line, evidence the concept is commercially viable, not just a startup pitch.
insights.quote: It was a very expensive toaster, but people referenced its ‘flight attendant call button’ sound
insights.locator: It was a very expensive toaster, but people referenced its

insights.claim: Hughes predicts that appliance makers' recent focus on sound as a purchase-driving 'delighter' is trickling down from high-margin premium product lines into the broader lineup, including ordinary microwaves.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A forward-looking signal that better sound design could become a broader appliance-category trend and competitive differentiator worth watching in upcoming product launches, not a one-off gimmick.
insights.quote: Companies have been focusing on product lines with more margin, but you're going to see that cascading into the microwave.

insights.claim: Starling, a two-person studio whose past clients include Sony, Microsoft, Netflix, Sega, and Ford, is publicizing its microwave sound experiments and says it isn't worried about manufacturers copying the technique in-house, betting that its design sensibility and consulting expertise are more valuable and defensible than any single sound.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: An unusually open, non-defensive IP posture from a small studio betting on ongoing consulting/services revenue over protecting a specific technique, relevant as a model for other small firms pitching big OEMs.
insights.quote: It's not a big fear that someone's going to steal this
insights.locator: It's not a big fear that someone's going to steal this

insights.claim: Starling says it already has a list of other hated everyday device sounds it wants to tackle next, beyond microwaves.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Signals Starling may expand its firmware-only sonic-UX fix model into adjacent device categories; worth watching for its next target and any manufacturer partnerships.
insights.locator: So, now that microwaves are sorted, what's next?
